**PURPOSE: Detects unreliable LLM-judge predictions on web-agent trajectories that arise from manipulated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning.**

The purpose is to detect when an LLM judge's prediction is unreliable due to CoT manipulation. Paper [4] investigates vulnerability of LLM-as-a-Judge to prompt-injection attacks, but its purpose is to *attack* not *defend/detect*. Paper [6] similarly proposes an attack. Paper [2] benchmarks instance-level faithfulness of CoT, which is about measuring faithfulness rather than detecting unreliable judge predictions from adversarial manipulation. Paper [3] studies inducing deceptive reasoning in LLMs — again, attack-side. Paper [11] evaluates defenses against IPI attacks on LLM agents, but focuses on bypassing defenses, not detecting unreliable judge outputs. None of the prior papers share the specific purpose of *detecting* unreliable LLM-judge predictions caused by manipulated CoT on web-agent trajectories. The closest is [2] (faithfulness detection) but it's about faithfulness benchmarking, not adversarial detection in judge settings.

**MECHANISM: Training-free two-stage framework comparing judgments from two counterfactual input views (with CoT vs without CoT) and selectively escalating disagreement cases to strict evidence-anchored evaluation.**

The core primitive is: compare outputs under two counterfactual input conditions (with/without CoT), detect disagreement, then escalate. Papers [9], [10], [12], [14], [16] cover selective prediction/classification with reject option — the "escalate disagreement cases" part maps onto selective prediction (abstain/escalate when uncertain). For mechanism equivalence at the primitive level: [17] uses differential testing (compare two views, flag disagreements) which is the core primitive here.
